title: What happens if a producer sends a message but no consumers are subscribed (retained per retention policy, not discarded like a queue)?
shortTitle: What happens if a producer sends a message but no consumers are subscribed
topicTitle: What happens if a producer sends a message but no consumers are subscribed

s1_definition.profdef: In Kafka, a producer writes records to a partition independently of whether any consumer exists. The record is appended to the partition's durable log and retained according to the topic's cleanup policy — by time and size for a delete policy, or latest-per-key for a compact policy — not until it is consumed. Consumption does not delete records. Therefore, if no consumer is subscribed when the record is produced, the record simply waits in the log, and whenever a consumer subscribes later it can read the record from the beginning of the retained log. This is fundamentally different from a traditional message queue, where a message with no consumer may be dropped or sits until exactly one consumer removes it.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India writes every transaction into a permanent ledger book, whether or not anyone is reading it right now. If the fraud analyst is on holiday when Rajesh makes a transfer, the entry is still written into the ledger and stays there. When the analyst comes back next week, they open the ledger and read everything that happened while they were away. Nothing was lost just because nobody was watching at that moment. A traditional queue would be like a to-do basket where a slip is thrown away if nobody is around to grab it — Kafka's ledger does not work that way.
s1_definition.oneliner: The record is durably retained in the log per the retention policy and waits for any future consumer; consumption never deletes it, unlike a queue.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** In Kafka, a producer writes records to a partition independently of whether any consumer exists. The record is appended to the partition's durable log and retained according to the topic's cleanup policy — by time and size for a delete policy, or latest-per-key for a compact policy — not until it is consumed. Consumption does not delete records. Therefore, if no consumer is subscribed when the record is produced, the record simply waits in the log, and whenever a consumer subscribes later it can read the record from the beginning of the retained log. This is fundamentally different from a traditional message queue, where a message with no consumer may be dropped or sits until exactly one consumer removes it.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India writes every transaction into a permanent ledger book, whether or not anyone is reading it right now. If the fraud analyst is on holiday when Rajesh makes a transfer, the entry is still written into the ledger and stays there. When the analyst comes back next week, they open the ledger and read everything that happened while they were away. Nothing was lost just because nobody was watching at that moment. A traditional queue would be like a to-do basket where a slip is thrown away if nobody is around to grab it — Kafka's ledger does not work that way.

**One line to remember:** The record is durably retained in the log per the retention policy and waits for any future consumer; consumption never deletes it, unlike a queue.

sections.s2_technical:
The core idea is that Kafka decouples producers from consumers through a durable log. When a producer calls `kafkaTemplate.send("transfers", key, value)`, the broker appends the record to the appropriate partition and assigns it an offset. This write succeeds and is acknowledged based solely on the producer's acks setting and the replication state — it has nothing to do with whether any consumer group exists or is online. So a producer can publish to a brand-new topic that no consumer has ever subscribed to, and the record is safely stored.

Retention, not consumption, governs the record's lifetime. With the default delete policy, the record lives until it exceeds `retention.ms` (for example seven days) or the partition exceeds `retention.bytes`. With a compact policy, the latest record per key is kept indefinitely. In neither case does reading a record remove it. This is the defining difference from a classic point-to-point queue like a traditional JMS queue or AWS SQS, where a message is typically removed once a consumer acknowledges it, and where a message produced with no consumer either waits for the single consumer or, in some fire-and-forget setups, is lost.

Because records persist regardless of consumers, a consumer that subscribes later can choose where to start reading using the `auto.offset.reset` setting. If set to `earliest`, a new consumer group with no committed offset starts from the very beginning of the retained log and reads every record still present, including those produced while no consumer existed. If set to `latest`, the new group starts only from records produced after it subscribes, effectively skipping the backlog. This is a crucial configuration: a fraud team that comes online later and needs the full recent history uses earliest, while a live dashboard that only cares about new events uses latest.

This decoupling is also what enables multiple independent consumer groups and replay. Since the record stays in the log, any number of groups can read it at their own pace, and a group can even rewind to re-read old records by seeking to an earlier offset. A record produced with no consumer is not a special or error case in Kafka; it is the normal, expected behavior of a log. The producer does not block, does not fail, and does not need a consumer to be present.

There are a few practical caveats. The record is only kept as long as retention allows, so if no consumer reads it for longer than the retention window, it will eventually be deleted by the cleanup policy — not because it was unconsumed, but because it aged out. Also, a consumer only receives records produced to partitions it is assigned, and offset resets only apply when there is no committed offset for that group. The senior-level nuance is that this log-centric model is precisely why Kafka suits event streaming, event sourcing, and audit: the data is a durable record of what happened, available to current and future consumers alike, rather than a transient task handed to one worker and then discarded.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India produces transaction events continuously, but some consuming teams are not always online, and the team must prove no events are lost just because a consumer was absent.

Problem 1 — The payments service produces transfer events around the clock, but the fraud analytics consumer is deployed later in the day. The transfers produced before fraud comes online must still be available. This is exactly Kafka's durable log with retention — records are written and retained regardless of consumers.

Problem 2 — When the fraud consumer finally starts, it must read everything that happened while it was offline, not just new events. This is exactly auto.offset.reset=earliest for a brand-new consumer group.

Problem 3 — A live dashboard, by contrast, only cares about events from now onward and should skip the backlog. This is exactly auto.offset.reset=latest.

The mini-project simulates this. We build a `TransferEvent` domain object, a `DurableLog` that appends records with offsets and enforces a retention window, and two late subscribers: an `EarliestConsumer` that reads from offset zero and a `LatestConsumer` that reads only from the current end. The demo produces several transfers with no consumer present, then subscribes both consumers and shows the earliest one reading the backlog while the latest one reads only new events, plus an event aged out by retention.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is four transfer events produced over time, with no consumer present at first, a retention window of 50 units, and a current time of 100.

Step 1 — With no consumer subscribed, the producer writes TXF-1 at time 40, TXF-2 at 70, and TXF-3 at 90. Each append succeeds and is stored at an offset in the durable log. The absence of a consumer has no effect on the writes; the records simply sit in the log.

Step 2 — Retention runs at time 100 with a window of 50, so the cutoff is time 50. TXF-1 at time 40 is older than the cutoff and is removed because it aged out, not because it was unconsumed. TXF-2 and TXF-3 survive. This shows that records are governed by retention, not consumption.

Step 3 — The fraud team comes online as a brand-new consumer group with auto.offset.reset=earliest. Because it has no committed offset, it starts from offset zero and reads the entire retained backlog — TXF-2 and TXF-3 — even though these were produced while no consumer existed. Nothing was lost; the fraud team catches up fully.

Step 4 — A new transfer TXF-4 is produced at time 101, after both teams exist, and is appended to the log.

Step 5 — The dashboard comes online as another new group with auto.offset.reset=latest. It starts at the current end offset, deliberately skipping the backlog, so it would only read records produced after it subscribed. The logs show the earliest consumer reading everything retained and the latest consumer skipping the backlog, proving that Kafka retains records for future consumers rather than discarding them like a queue.

```

```

```
  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Publish-Subscribe over a durable log (not a queue)           │
  │    WHY: records survive for current AND future subscribers   │
  │ Strategy: offset-reset strategy (earliest vs latest)         │
  │    WHY: a late consumer chooses backlog or only-new          │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: DurableLog stores+ages; consumers only read               │
  │ O: new consumer type = new class, log unchanged              │
  │ D: consumers depend on the DurableLog abstraction            │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ───────────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │          DurableLog           │
  │ - topic, retentionWindow      │
  │ - records: List<TransferEvent>│
  │ - timestamps: List<Long>      │
  │ ──────────────────────────────│
  │ + append(event, ts): void     │  succeeds with no consumer
  │ + runRetention(now): void     │  age-out only
  │ + endOffset(): int; at(off)   │
  └──────────────┬────────────────┘
      ┌──────────┴──────────────┐ read
      ▼                         ▼
  ┌──────────────────┐   ┌──────────────────┐
  │ EarliestConsumer │   │ LatestConsumer   │
  │ + subscribeAndRead│   │ + subscribeAndRead│
  │   from offset 0  │   │   from endOffset  │
  └──────────────────┘   └──────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: a produced record ──────────────────────────

  [PRODUCED (no consumer)] → [RETAINED in log]
     → consumer subscribes (earliest) → [READ from backlog]
     → never read + age > retention → [DELETED by retention]
  (consumption never deletes; only retention does)

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────────

  1. logTopic.append(TXF-1..3)  (no consumer) → all STORED
  2. logTopic.runRetention(now=100) → TXF-1 aged out
  3. new EarliestConsumer("fraud").subscribeAndRead() → TXF-2, TXF-3
  4. logTopic.append(TXF-4)
  5. new LatestConsumer("dashboard").subscribeAndRead() → start at end

  Contract for append(event, ts):
    Pre:  topic exists
    Post: record stored and retained per policy, regardless of consumers
    Rule: readers do not affect storage; only retention removes records
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
If a producer sends a message but no consumer is subscribed, the message is not lost — this is one of the most important differences between Kafka and a traditional queue. In Kafka a producer writes to a partition completely independently of whether any consumer exists. The broker appends the record to the durable log, assigns it an offset, and acknowledges the write based only on the acks and replication state, not on the presence of a consumer. The record then simply waits in the log.

How long it waits is governed by the retention policy, not by consumption. With the default delete policy, the record lives until it exceeds retention.ms or the partition exceeds retention.bytes; with a compact policy, the latest record per key is kept. Reading a record never deletes it. This is the opposite of a classic point-to-point queue, where a message is removed once a consumer acknowledges it and may be dropped if no consumer is around in a fire-and-forget setup.

Because records persist regardless of consumers, a consumer that subscribes later controls where it starts with auto.offset.reset. A brand-new group with earliest reads the entire retained backlog, including everything produced while no consumer existed, while a group with latest starts from the current end and skips the backlog. This same log-centric design is what lets many independent consumer groups read the same records and lets a group rewind to replay history.

In my banking platform at National Bank of India, the payments service produces transfer events around the clock, and the fraud analytics consumer is sometimes deployed later in the day. Because the events are retained in the log, when the fraud consumer comes online as a new group with earliest, it reads every transfer that happened while it was offline, so nothing is missed. A live dashboard, by contrast, uses latest because it only cares about new events. The senior point I always make is that a record produced with no consumer is not an error or special case in Kafka — it is the normal behavior of a durable log, and that is exactly why Kafka is ideal for event streaming, event sourcing, and audit, where the data is a lasting record of what happened rather than a transient task handed to one worker. The only real caveat is that a record still ages out if it sits unread longer than the retention window, which is a retention decision, not a consumption one.
